title: Research
text:
Draft, October 2026 · Code
Brazilian depositors leave most of their balances in accounts that pay well below the policy rate, even though better-paying deposits are one transfer away and the Pix instant-payment system made that transfer free. I ask which friction keeps them in place: inattention, unawareness of alternatives, the cost of moving, or an informed preference to stay.
I extend the dynamic deposit model of Egan, Hortaçsu, Kaplan, Sunderam, and Yao (2025) to a market where brick-and-mortar banks compete locally and digital banks nationally, with random-coefficients (BLP) demand. Estimation proceeds in two steps on a municipality-level panel of bank balances built from Banco Central do Brasil supervisory data (2016–2024): depositor sleepiness from the persistence of deposits, with a control function for endogenous spreads, and demand from a BLP contraction.
Preliminary findings

Over a full year, 94.3 percent of balances are never re-optimized (98.6 percent in a given quarter), and inertia is deeper in poorer markets.
Active depositors’ mean own-price elasticity is −0.46, but because most balances are asleep, the deposit base responds to a spread change on impact with an elasticity of only −0.01. This gap is the market power that inertia gives incumbent banks.
The launch of Pix is associated with a reduction in the sleepy share of 0.6 percentage points, not distinguishable from zero (95 percent interval [−3.9, 0.2]). The interval is too wide to rule out a large rise in the share of depositors who shop.
A market’s 2019 mobile access predicts its Pix use, which gives a first step toward separating attention from the cost of moving money.

title: Pedro Feijó de Moraes
text:
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Economics at Yale University, working in industrial organization and financial economics. My research studies competition in retail banking: why depositors leave their money in low-yield accounts, and how much market power that inertia gives banks. I combine dynamic structural models of demand with large administrative datasets from the Banco Central do Brasil.
During my undergraduate studies, I spent a year as a macroeconomics research intern at Bahia Asset Management, where I ran GDP and CPI nowcasting models and maintained the cross-country database used by the research team and the trading desk. I hold an M.A. in Economics from FGV EPGE and placed first nationally in Brazil’s 2019 ANPEC graduate entrance exam in economics.
You can reach me at pedro.feijodemoraes@yale.edu.
